extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (epistemology/metaphysics); those studying Locke's theory of ideas and substance
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying John Locke's criteria about how complex ideas (mixed modes, substances) are formed, named, and understood — useful for critique, summary, or peer-review of philosophical argumentation about ideas and substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming mixed modes driven by frequency/utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of language is to mark, or communicate men's thoughts to one another with all the dispatch that may be, they usually make SUCH collections of ideas into complex modes, and affix names to them, as they have frequent use of in their way of living and conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke explains that combinations of simple ideas become settled 'mixed modes' and receive names when they are frequently needed in daily life; rare combinations remain unnamed and are instead described by enumerating constituent ideas to avoid burdening memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language-specific complex ideas (untranslatable words)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are in every language many particular words which cannot be rendered by any one single word of another, because several fashions, customs, and manners of one nation make several combinations of ideas familiar to one people and not to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: Greek 'ostrakismos' and Roman 'proscriptio' stand for complex ideas not present in other nations. Implication: lexical gaps reflect differing customary combinations of ideas; translators must often use periphrasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Languages change via new complex modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Languages constantly change, take up new and lay by old terms, because change of customs and opinions brings new combinations of ideas which it is necessary frequently to think on and talk about, so new names are annexed to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke points to the practical economy of speech: new social or conceptual needs generate new named complex ideas (e.g., 'reprieve' or 'appeal' compress many ideas into a short sound).

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of mixed modes often mistaken for ideas themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed modes, being fleeting and transient combinations of simple ideas, have not so much any constant existence anywhere but in the minds of men, and therefore we are apt to annex them to the names that excite them in us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the names of mixed modes persist more steadily than the mental combination, people may mistake the name for the idea itself; e.g., the ideas of 'triumph' or 'apotheosis' do not exist all at once in things, yet their names give them apparent stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of complex ideas (three ways)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three ways whereby we get these complex ideas of mixed modes: (1) By experience and OBSERVATION of things themselves; (2) By INVENTION, or voluntary putting together of several simple ideas in our own minds; (3) By EXPLAINING THE NAMES of actions we never saw, or motions we cannot see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke illustrates each: observing two men wrestle yields the idea of wrestling; inventing printing precedes its existence; and explaining a name by enumerating its constituent ideas allows one to form the complex idea (example: analysis of the mixed mode 'lie').

rubrics_metrics.name: All complex ideas ultimately resolvable into simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: All our complex ideas are ultimately resolvable into simple ideas, of which they are compounded and originally made up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke emphasizes reduction: even if immediate ingredients are themselves complex, ultimately they trace back to simple ideas obtained from sensation or reflection; this underpins his epistemological method of analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain simple ideas most prolific in making mixed modes
rubrics_metrics.description: It is worth observing which of all our simple ideas have been MOST modified, and had most mixed ideas made out of them: THINKING and MOTION (which comprehend all action), and POWER, from whence these actions are conceived to flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because action is central to human affairs, many named mixed modes derive from variations on thinking, motion, and power (examples: boldness, habit, disposition, testiness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Words seeming to signify action often signify only the effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Many words which seem to express some action, signify nothing of the action or MODUS OPERANDI at all, but barely the effect, with some circumstances of the subject wrought on, or cause operating: e.g. CREATION, ANNIHILATION, freezing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke warns against inferring knowledge of causal mechanisms from ordinary language; terms can name results without conveying the manner in which they are produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed modes arise from more than power/action
rubrics_metrics.description: Though power and action make the greatest part of mixed modes, other simple ideas, and their several combinations, are not excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke notes that a full accounting would require a dictionary of many words used in divinity, ethics, law, and politics—mixed modes are diverse in origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of the idea of substance: co-occurrence => substratum
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind takes notice that a certain number of simple ideas go constantly together; which being presumed to belong to one thing, and words being suited to common apprehensions, are called, so united in one subject, by one name; and by inadvertency we are apt afterward to talk of and consider them as one simple idea, calling that supposed support SUBSTANCE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues that the idea of 'substance' is a mental hypothesis to account for regularly co-occurring qualities; this is an explanatory fiction rather than a clear positive idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscure idea of substance in general ('something I know not what')
rubrics_metrics.description: If one examines the notion of pure substance in general, one will find he has no other idea of it than a supposition of he knows not what SUPPORT of such qualities which are capable of producing simple ideas in us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke uses the child's answer 'something' to show lack of clear conception; the general idea of substance is essentially obscure and denotes ignorance about the underlying bearer of qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular substances are specific collections of simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Our ideas of PARTICULAR SORTS OF SUBSTANCES are by collecting SUCH combinations of simple ideas as are, by experience and observation, taken notice of to exist together; and are therefore supposed to flow from the particular internal constitution, or unknown essence of that substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the idea of 'swan' is white colour, long neck, red beak, black legs, swimming power, etc.; a subject's 'idea' is a bundle of observed qualities rather than knowledge of an essence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active and passive powers form part of complex ideas of substances
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideas that make our complex ones of corporeal substances include primary qualities, sensible secondary qualities, and the aptness in any substance to give or receive alterations (active and passive powers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke treats powers (e.g., a loadstone's power to draw iron; gold's power to be melted but not consumed) as constituent ideas because they are discovered through sensible effects; powers function as characteristic notes for distinguishing substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary qualities are powers dependent on primary qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The sensible secondary qualities, depending on primary qualities, are nothing but the powers those substances have to produce several ideas in us by our senses; these ideas are not in the things themselves, otherwise than as anything is in its cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke distinguishes primary (bulk, figure, motion) as really in bodies, from secondary (colour, taste) which are powers to produce ideas in observers; this has implications for how we ascribe properties to objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three components of corporeal-substance ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideas that make our complex ones of corporeal substances are of these three sorts: (1) ideas of the primary qualities (bulk, figure, number, situation, motion); (2) sensible secondary qualities (powers to produce ideas in us); (3) the aptness to give/receive alterations (active/passive powers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tripartite account organizes how to analyze any corporeal substance's idea; Locke repeatedly recommends attending to these categories when forming distinct notions of substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Our sensory limitations shape which qualities we notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Had we senses acute enough to discern the minute particles of bodies and the real constitution on which their sensible qualities depend, many secondary qualities would disappear and our ideas of substances would differ greatly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke uses microscope examples: sand appears white to naked eye but pellucid under magnification; this supports the criterion that what we count as properties depends on the scale and acuity of our perceptual apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human faculties suited to life, not perfect knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The contriver of us has fitted our senses, faculties, and organs to the conveniences of life; we are furnished with faculties to discover enough in the creatures to lead us to the knowledge of the Creator and our duty, but not to a perfect, clear, and adequate knowledge of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical adequacy, not epistemic completeness, explains why our ideas are limited; an evaluator should keep in mind Locke's teleological account of faculties when assessing claims about the scope of human knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity of idea-clarity for spiritual and corporeal substances
rubrics_metrics.description: We have as clear an idea of an immaterial spirit as of material substance because both ideas are formed by putting together ideas (thinking, perceiving, liberty, power of moving) plus the obscure notion of 'substance' as support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues symmetry: lack of a clear idea of substance affects both body and spirit equally; this undermines claims that corporeal substance is intrinsically more intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: No abstract idea of substance (either body or spirit)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no idea of abstract substance either in body or spirit; our idea of substance is always confused—the supposed support of qualities—so we have no clear abstract conception of substance itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This cautions against positing an abstract substratum beyond the bundle of observable or experiential qualities; evaluators should avoid treating 'substance' as a positively known entity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing marks: cohesion & impulse vs thinking & will
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary ideas peculiar to body are the COHESION OF SOLID, AND CONSEQUENTLY SEPARABLE, PARTS, and a POWER OF COMMUNICATING MOTION BY IMPULSE; those peculiar to spirit are THINKING and WILL (a power of putting body into motion and liberty); existence, duration, and mobility are common to both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these criteria to differentiate discourse about bodies versus spirits: bodies characterized by separable solidity and impulse-transmitted motion, spirits by mental activity and volition; Locke grounds these as the clearest distinctive ideas available.
